Issued at 237 AM CDT Tue Sep 15 2026

The last of the lingering areas of mist across western WI are 
departing eastward at this hour. Satellite offers a bit of a mixed 
bag, with low stratus across central/eastern MN and western WI. On 
the flip side, skies have cleared across southwestern MN which has 
allowed for the development of patchy fog. The continued eastward 
movement of an upper-low across Manitoba will drag a trailing cold 
front eastward through daybreak. The frontal passage will work to 
flush out low clouds/fog and will turn the winds out of the WNW. It 
will be a breezy first half of the day as gusts reach speeds between 
25-30 mph (strongest across central MN through midday). Winds will 
decrease as the surface pressure gradient softens this afternoon. 
Otherwise, it should be a nice day with highs in the upper 60s/lower 
70s under mostly sunny skies.

Eastward expansion of surface high pressure will result in clear 
skies and light winds tonight, allowing for tonight's lows to run on 
the cooler side of guidance. The coolest portion of the forecast 
area will be communities north of I-94 in central MN/western WI. 
Lows in the lower 40s to perhaps a few upper 30s are expected in 
these locations.

Large scale view captures ~600 dm ridge remaining locked in place 
across the southeastern CONUS through the end of the week. Today's 
front will continue southeastward before stalling across the Ohio 
Valley as it approaches the ridge. At the same time, upper-level 
southwesterly flow will send a series of shortwaves across the 
Plains, eventually lifting northeast around the western periphery
of the ridge. The first shortwave is progged to move across the
Plains Wednesday and will produce rain across Iowa in association
with the stalled out boundary. We'll carry slight chance to chance
PoPs Wednesday for scattered showers mainly for the southern half
of the forecast area. Additionally, a weak northern stream wave
progged to move through ND/northwest MN may support a few 
showers across the northern portion of the forecast area, but 
these chances appear to be lower. Overall, Wednesday will be 
mainly dry with low impact shower chances.

Thursday will be dry and slightly warmer (mid to upper 70s) as mid-
level warm advection increases ahead of the next wave. A ~40kt LLJ 
is progged to develop across the eastern Plains in advance of the 
next upper-level shortwave that will move from the central 
Plains into southern MN on Friday. Anomalous moisture advection 
(PWATs of ~2"+) and isentropic ascent will result in development
of a broad precipitation shield and guidance has continued to 
trend upwards in the QPF category. As mentioned by the previous
discussion, the key factor of uncertainty at this point is how 
far north/south the heaviest precipitation axis will setup. For
being 3-4 days out, a reasonable degree of spread exists across
the guidance suite. Various deterministic solutions feature a 
much needed swath of 1-3" across much of the MPX forecast area. 
However, there are a number of ensemble members that advertise 
a more southerly solution that places the swath of heaviest rain
along the MN/IA border. Adding to the uncertainty is the 
machine learning guidance (in particular the AIFS) which have 
leaned on the side of the more southern solution. Putting the 
pieces together, it's looking increasingly likely that Friday 
will feature another round of widespread rain...it's just a 
question of how far north/south the heaviest axis of rainfall 
sets up. Our latest PoP grids from the NBM appears to merge the 
two model "camps" together, with a highest PoPs (90-100%) 
located along and south of I-94. A few stronger storms will be
possible near the surface warm front, which looks to lift as far
north as the MN/IA border. 

To sum it up, prospects of soaking/beneficial rainfall on Friday 
are increasing across our forecast area, but uncertainty 
regarding latitudinal placement of the heaviest precipitation 
swath remains the primary forecast challenge. In other words, 
the setup is there, we just need things to keep trending in the 
right direction! 

The weekend forecast is trending drier, though the approach of a 
weakening upper-low across the Dakotas may support the development 
of warm advective showers on Sunday. Guidance shows the upper-
low meandering over the Upper Midwest into early next week, 
which supports highs in the upper 60s to lower 70s through the 
end of the period.
